newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russian premier says getting Olympics "political".
newsitem.headline: Russian premier says getting Olympics "political".

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday his country's bid to win the 2004 Olympic Games for St Petersburg was linked to its drive to become a "normal, civilised society".

Chernomyrdin, speaking during a visit to the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), said that for Russia the Olympic movement represented not only culture and education but also "the purity of the nation".
"This is a political question, I cannot hide it," he told reporters after talks with IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch on the candidacy of Russia's second city for the Games in eight years' time.

"Russia has taken the path of democracy, of creating a market economy," Chernomyrdin said. "We want to be a normal, civilised society. Our choice is for all time, and the processes that have been started in Russia are irreversible.
"The holding of the Olympic Games (in St Petersburg) would be a forum that would give worldwide recognition of that fact."

Chernomyrdin, nominated to stand in as head of state when President Boris Yeltsin undergoes a heart operation in the coming weeks, recognised that there was stiff opposition facing the northern city, formerly Leningrad.
"It will not be easy for the IOC to choose," he said. "There are a lot of things that have to be taken into account."

Samaranch, standing alongside the Russian prime minister, was noncommittal. "We are very much impressed by the full support of the Russian government for the bid of St Petersburg," said the former Spanish diplomat and ex-ambassador to Moscow.
A total of 10 other cities are in the race for the 2004 Games, among which the strong favourites at present are believed to be Rome, Cape Town and Stockholm.
A list of four or five finalists is due to be decided by the IOC next March and the winner will be announced in September 1997. The next Games will be held in Sydney in the year 2000.

Chernomyrdin, who earlier in the day had held talks with Jean-Pascale Delamuraz, current holder of Switzerland's rotating presidency, rejected suggestions from a Russian journalist that the Games might be too costly.
"Holding the Olympics and similar events does not wreck budgets, quite the reverse, it gives them a boost," he declared.
"It is very important not only for St Petersburg but also for Russia....and I think the world at large would gain a lot from holding the Games in a city which has won world renown for its culture."

Russian officials are known to be keen to bring the Games to their country to try to wipe out memories of the 1980 Olympics in Moscow, then capital of the old Soviet Union, which were held under the shadow of political controversies.
The United States and several other countries boycotted the event as a protest against the Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan the previous year.

The Soviet authorities were also widely criticised for clearing the city of political dissidents and for barring people from surrounding regions from the city while the Games were on. Those people then travelled regularly to Moscow for food supplies.
